title: The Dothan hotel, a burned mattress, and the bellboy years later
summary: Staying in a white hotel as an Indian, Moore burned a mattress, left quietly, and was asked about it by the bellboy when he played Dothan with Armstrong.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Did you ever have any trouble along the road or when you were playing some of these joints, you know, as far as accommodations and that sort of thing. Well, I mean, it's sort of a question that answers itself for musicians before the 1960s.

There was one time, we were playing Dothan, Alabama, and there's no black hotel in Dothan so everyone is staying at private homes that take care of the musicians except that one guy, Foots. Foots didn't have a room at all, he couldn't find a vacant room anywhere so I gave up my room and gave my room to Foots. I went down to the hotel in there and I went to the lobby and this old white fella come to meet me and said, "What are you?" I said, "I'm a full-blooded American Indian." He said, "I thought so," he said, "You know, by God, my folks were part Indian, too. I'm part Indian myself. Of course you

can stay here. Come on in. Sign up." I think I was kind of loaded that night and it kind of rubbed me the wrong way because he accepted me because I was Indian, you know. They should accept everybody else. So I got my room and I was up in the room and I must have fell asleep but in other words I may have misgivings about my attitude toward staying in this hotel, I happened to smoke in bed and I burned a mattress and I woke up in time to go to the corner and get glasses of water to throw the fire out, I got the fire out and I opened up the rear window, but you could see the smoke all over the room. So in about an hour or two I said, I better get out of here before I get in trouble. So I dressed and coming down there's the same guy downstairs, he says, "Are you leaving already?" I said, "Yes, I got a long ways to go back to Oklahoma."

And he looked at me and then he says to me, "Do you smell smoke?" I said, "No, do you?" He says, "Yeah, I smell smoke." I guess it was in my clothes. I said, well, call the fire department or something. I said, "No, I don't think so, there doesn't seem to be any fire." The gist of it was I went back to my part of town and doubled in with somebody there for the rest

of the morning. But the end of the story, of this segment continues until the next three or four years when I was with Armstrong and we played Dothan, Alabama, and we played in the Armory there with Satchmo. I was sitting up there on the bandstand and off to one side was a table. And it was a black dance. The whites were up there in the balcony, but downstairs the blacks had their tables and the booze and setups and what-have-you. One fella came to me and said, "Hey, have you been here before?" I said, "No." I began to get apprehensive. "There was a guy here and he looked just like you. He nearly burned a hotel. And I said, "How did he burn the hotel?" "He set the mattress on fire. Are you sure you haven't been here before?" I said, "No." How do you know he burned it?" "Because I was the bellboy down there and they told me about it when I came to work that morning and they described who he looked like and the guy looked like you and I thought you might have been here." I said, "No, no, it wasn't me." I'll never forget that.
He tried to catch up on you.
He did, but I didn't let him know it. I'll never forget that.
